sections.text: As a ship at sea is tossed by the tempest, so the reason is carried away by the mind when preyed upon by straying senses.
Therefore, O Might-in-Arms, he who keeps his senses detached from their objects - take it that his reason is purified.
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।
The saint is awake when the world sleeps, and he ignores that for which the world lives.

We had been discussing Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge. Bhagavan gave us a roadmap for our journey from ignorance about ourselves to the knowledge of the Supreme. We have seen this step by step.
How can I come out of this ignorance about myself? Right now I consider this body as me, this mind as me, this intellect as me. Ideas such as I think, therefore I am create attachment to my mind and my intellect. And this body serves as my vehicle for all my experiences in this world, which creates attachment to it.
Therefore I consider the death of this body to be my death. I have not seen anybody coming back after he dies, so I conclude the death of this body is my death. But Bhagavan said, dehinosmin yatha dehe kaumaram yauvanam jara tatha dehantara praptir dhiras tatra na muhyati.
Just as you have seen changes in your life from childhood to youth to old age, you should not be confused by the transition to another body. You have seen in your journey various states of existence. You existed as a child, as a youth, and also as an old man.
Now he said, youre not confused by that, that does not delude you. These experiences which are different from each other has never confused you, who you are. You always consider, this is me.
When I say I, it remains same no matter what state I was in, whether I was a child, a young man or an old man. Since those changes in this life did not confuse you about who you are, the change to another body also should not confuse you. This is a hypothesis for us now because we do not have direct experience of it.
But the idea of reincarnation was introduced to us: that this life is not the only life. You lived many lives before, where you created all your vasanas and tendencies. I have a tendency to be artistic, somebody else has a tendency to be athletic, another person is more intellectual.
Where are all these tendencies coming from? Bhagavan said these tendencies come from your experiences in past lives, before you were even born in this body. And then he basically said that this journey is one of activity. In this journey you have to be active all your life.
Then the question is: how do I act in this world? Bhagavan said, sukha duhkhe same kritva labha alabha jayajayau, tato yuddhaya yujyasva -- with a balanced mind you should act in this world. Thats basically simple advice Bhagavan gave. Samatvam Yoga Uchate.
Create balance in your mind in all the various experiences youre experiencing. And then you will be on your path to your destination. Your destination is to find perfect happiness.
Bhagawan said you will find that if you act in this world with a balanced mind. Then my question is: how do I keep a balanced mind with varied experiences in my life? And Bhagawan said Yukta Asita Matparaha. Keep an overarching goal which encompasses everything -- all your experiences, all your feelings, and all your thoughts.
Then you will be able to balance your mind. If you have an overarching goal, then that goal becomes the destination. The goal will be reflected in all your experiences.
We have all experienced that when you are in love, when you are fixated with one object, you see that in everything. When you fall in love, you see that person. In all other persons you see -- that must be her, that must be him. Because my mind is so overpowered by that goal that I see everything in it.
When I become a father or mother for the first time, in all children I see my child. Then when I first become a grandfather, I see my granddaughter and grandson in all children. Because whatever is taking over your mind, you will reflect that in all your experiences.
If your mind is focused on Me, if I am your supreme goal, then I will be reflected in all your experiences. Everything I see, I will see His manifestation. Everything I hear, I will hear His voice, His flute in that sound.
So everything will become divine. The experience may be anything, but now my mind will not assign any value other than a divine value to it. Bhagavan said Yukta Asita Matparaha -- but to become Yukta, to be established in that union, Bhagavan says Tani Sarvani Samyamya, you must control all your senses.
Vashe hi yasya indriyani -- one who has the senses under control. Tasya prajna pratishtita -- his wisdom is steady. What hes seeing is what is truly there to be seen.
When my wisdom is steady and my mind is balanced, Im seeing reality. If my wisdom is not steady, if I assign different values to different things based on my likes and dislikes, then my wisdom is not steady. The result of that would be that I will not have any Sukha, I will not be at peace.
So the last verse which we discussed says Nasti buddhir ayuktasya. One who has no overarching goal is Ayukta. Yukta is one who is identified with the supreme goal.
My supreme goal should be having Sukha and no Dukkha. That overarching goal in my life is to avoid Dukkha and have only ultimate happiness. That happens when you are identified with the supreme self.
Bhagavan says, the one who is not identified with the supreme goal is Ayukta. He has no fixed goal, so anything will become his goal. Whatever experience I have, Ill be attached to it, and then I will not know where my happiness truly lies.
It is something like when I was in India or in Africa -- there were only a few choices, like two or three: Kesar, Pista, or Kajudraks ice cream. When I went to Law Garden in Ahmedabad, the choices were very clear, not really a big question mark. But I come here and Baskin Robbins has 31 flavors.
Now how do I know which flavor is best? If I taste all 31 of them, by the time I get to the 31st flavor, I forget what the first flavor tasted like. I would have to start all over again. So I really have no clue where my happiness lies.
Because every time I taste something, I think thats it. And then I say, but there are 30 other flavors. I need to try them also.
Maybe there is one better than this. So Bhagavan said, one who is Ayukta -- who does not have this fixed goal of what he is trying to achieve -- he will not have any Buddhi. Nasti buddhir ayuktasya.
He does not have the wisdom to know what his goal is and where his happiness lies. He also does not have any firm identification; his identification shifts from one goal to another. In one who is not identified with one goal, how can there be any peace? His mind is agitated.
Even when Im achieving something, I think, This may not be it. There may be other things which other people are getting that Im not getting. I should be going after them.
I may be missing out on something. So Bhagavan said, na cabhavayatah shantih. One who does not have identification with his goal has no Shanti. And ashantasya kutah sukham -- for the one who is agitated, where is happiness? We all know this: when the mind is agitated, there is no Sukha.
Sukha I only experience when there is no agitating thought in my mind. Used to say: I minus I want equals happiness. As long as there is I want, there cannot be any happiness.
As long as Im wanting something, there cannot be any peace in my mind, because theres agitation -- I dont have it. I must be doing something which is not right. Or I may not be doing something which I should be doing now. Those thoughts create ashanti.
Such a person cannot have Sukham. If your goal is to achieve Sukha, you need to quieten your mind. And then Bhagavan explains why it is very important that you start with controlling your senses, which we have seen earlier.
Dhyayato visayan pumsah -- if I let my senses get impressions of the sense objects, then I keep thinking about them, and then Ill fall down that ladder of fall. So it says Indriyanam hi charatam yan manonuvidhiyate -- if my mind follows the wandering senses. Senses are involuntarily going out and getting impressions of the objects they are contacting.
If I keep my eyes open and see outside the window, there will be an impression of whats outside. But what I actually see depends on the disposition of my mind. For example, I see my friend Omi Narayan every day posting pictures of birds or flowers on his Facebook.
But when I look outside, I see buildings. I say, Well, that guys house looks nice, but I think it could have been designed a little better than this. So the disposition of my mind is to see the built world, not the natural world, even though were both looking outside. The senses are involuntarily going out there and getting impressions of these sense objects.
It is the mind which creates meaning from those impressions. Indriyanam hi charatam -- these wandering senses go out, and if the mind follows these wandering senses, getting attached to each object it perceives and wanting to keep thinking about it, then tadasya harati prajnam -- it carries away his wisdom. Now he obviously does not have the discrimination to know what is right and what is wrong for him, what to accept and what to reject.
A picture is worth a thousand words, so Bhagavan gives this image: just as a boat on the waters with no controller, no boatman, just a boat by itself -- it will be tossed by the wind. Wherever the wind takes it, it will go. There is no fixed destination.
If your mind follows every object which is perceived through the senses, then it will be tossed from one object to another. It does not have a goal and therefore it does not have any destination. My destination was happiness, but I lost my way because I have not fixed my destination.
I do not know where to go. I am just driving but do not know where I am going. And then Bhagavan says Tasmad yasya mahabaho -- therefore, O Mighty-Armed.
Bhagawan gives Arjuna a little boost of courage: you are capable of doing this, of controlling your senses. Nigrihitani Sarvashah Indriyani Indriyarthebhyah. Therefore, one who has controlled all his senses from the sense objects -- Tasya Prajna Pratishtita -- his wisdom is steady.
This is a very difficult verse to understand because we think it is impossible -- impossible to not have any perception of this world outside. The very job of senses is to perceive the world outside. If my mind is completely inert and is not getting any impression, then Ill be basically a dead person., If thats the case, if youre not perceiving anything, just let us know and well do your last rites. So if thats what it means, it is not possible for us to do that.
The very nature of senses is to get impressions in the very nature of mind is to get attached to those impressions. But what I will see as my mind depends on the disposition of my mind. If I have already fixed a goal that my goal is to have ultimate happiness and therefore I have to fix my mind on the ultimate self, then I will see the manifestation of that self in everything which I hear, I taste, I touch.
So the people who are bhakta, when they listen to music, they see Krishna Bhakti in it. To them the music is for achieving Gods Bhakti. Otherwise I sing film songs and it has different emotions in it.

Verse 67 uses a powerful image: As a ship at sea is tossed by the tempest, so the reason is carried away by the mind when preyed upon by straying senses. Without mastery over the senses, even a wise persons discrimination can be swept away. The senses wander naturally toward their objects; if the mind follows them, wisdom is lost like a rudderless boat in a storm.
Verse 68 restates the requirement: He who keeps his senses detached from their objects - take it that his reason is purified. And verse 69 offers a striking paradox: The saint is awake when the world sleeps, and he ignores that for which the world lives. What ordinary people consider most real and important (sense pleasures, worldly success), the sage sees as relatively unreal - like being asleep to the deeper truth. Conversely, what the sage is awake to (the Self, the eternal) seems like nothing to ordinary perception.
This is an invitation to examine your own sleep and wakefulness. What consumes your attention and energy? Is it what the verse calls the worlds concerns, or something deeper? Try this contemplation: Imagine looking back at your current life from your deathbed. What that you now pursue will seem important then? What will seem like sleep-walking through life? The sage is awake now to what will matter then. Today, try to stay awake to what is truly significant amid the distractions that normally capture your attention.
